summary: Gives a framework for carrying ANSI C12.22 / IEEE 1703 / MC12.22 smart-meter messages over IP networks. It was written by participants in those groups, not as an official submission on their behalf. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Electricity meters have their own language. This describes how to send that language across the internet.

questions: how to send meter data over ip
subtitle: Carrying smart meter messages on IP networks.

tldr.problem: Smart electric meters use a specialized protocol called ANSI C12.22 that is designed to carry meter readings and other data. Utilities need to transport these meter messages over IP networks instead of only over proprietary networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines how C12.22 messages are transported using TCP and UDP over IP, including how to address meters using IP addresses and ports, handle multicast and broadcast, and ensure reliable or connectionless delivery.
tldr.outcome: Utilities can now build Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) systems where smart meters communicate over standard IP networks, though the application layer remains proprietary C12.22.

today: RFC 6142 is informational and describes existing practice in ANSI C12.22 and IEEE 1703 implementations. It remains the standard for transporting meter messages over IP networks and has not been superseded.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: ANSI C12.22 is an application layer protocol for smart meters and Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) systems. It is jointly published by ANSI, IEEE and Measurement Canada, with standards C12.19 (the data tables), C12.22 (the application protocol), IEEE 1377 and 1703, and MC12.19 and MC12.22 (the Measurement Canada variants). This RFC describes how to transport C12.22 messages over IP networks using TCP and UDP, mapping the protocol's native addressing scheme to IP addresses and ports.
sections.eli5: Smart meters talk in a special way that different meter companies all understand. This document explains how to make those meters talk to each other over the internet using regular internet rules.

sections.title: Native IP Addresses and Ports
sections.content: C12.22 nodes on an IP network are identified by a Native IP Address: a binary IP address (IPv4 or IPv6), an optional port number, and an optional protocol identifier (TCP or UDP). The default port for C12.22 is port 1153, registered with IANA for both TCP and UDP. When encoding a C12.22 address in the meter data tables, the address may be IPv4 alone (4 bytes), IPv4 plus port (6 bytes), or IPv4 plus port plus protocol (7 bytes); the same applies for IPv6 (16, 18, or 19 bytes respectively). All C12.22 IP nodes must have their IP address configured before sending or receiving messages.
sections.eli5: Each meter needs an address on the internet, just like your house has a street address. The standard gives them port 1153, which is like a suite number inside a building.

sections.title: TCP and UDP Transport
sections.content: C12.22 supports both TCP (connection-oriented) and UDP (connectionless) modes, controlled by configuration flags (CL for connectionless, CO for connection-oriented) in each node. A node can be Active-OPEN (initiates connections or sends unsolicited datagrams) or Passive-OPEN (listens for incoming traffic). TCP connections are bidirectional by default (recommended), but some implementations use them unidirectionally. For UDP, large messages (exceeding the path MTU) must be segmented using the C12.22 Datagram Segmentation and Reassembly algorithm. When a request is received, the response must use the same transport protocol (TCP to TCP, UDP to UDP), and in UDP the response is sent back to the requester's source IP and port.
sections.eli5: Messages can travel two ways: TCP is like a phone call where you know the other person got the message, and UDP is like sending a postcard where you just hope it arrives.

sections.title: Multicast and Broadcast
sections.content: C12.22 requires support for IP multicast to enable address discovery. When a node does not know the address of a relay or another meter, it can send a C12.22 Resolve Service Request using IP multicast to discover addresses on the LAN. IANA has assigned the multicast group 224.0.2.4 (IPv4) and FF0X::204 (IPv6, where X is the scope) for the All C1222 Nodes group. IPv4 relays control multicast scope using TTL (Time-to-Live) in the IP header; IPv6 nodes should use the minimum scope needed (link-local, admin-local, site-local, or organization-local). IP broadcast (255.255.255.255 in IPv4) is permitted only in controlled, private management domains; it is not supported in IPv6.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a meter doesn't know where to send a message, so it shouts to everyone on its network using multicast: 'Hey, does anyone know where meter XYZ is?' The right person answers.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: C12.22 defines application-layer security options: cleartext messages, authenticated plaintext, or authenticated ciphertext. When using cleartext, the network or transport layer should provide encryption. The RFC recommends that nodes encrypt key fields and mask passwords in read responses. Legacy deployments may not have security, but multi-homed nodes with Internet access must use C12.22 authentication and confidentiality. Additional transport-layer security (TLS, IPsec) may be applied transparently but must not alter or corrupt the C12.22 messages themselves. Key management details are outside the scope of C12.22 itself.
sections.eli5: The meters can scramble their messages using passwords, but they have to do it themselves—the internet doesn't know about meter passwords.
